unit_name: Area of Study 1: Western Classical Tradition 1650–1910
lesson_title: The Orchestra 1650-1910: How the Sound Changed
content_html:
Three orchestras, three sound worlds

Between 1650 and 1910 the orchestra changed almost beyond recognition. A Baroque band might have had a dozen players and a harpsichord. A late Romantic orchestra could field over a hundred. Section A of your listening exam plays short unfamiliar extracts from across this period and asks you to name the era, the instruments and the way the sound is built. This lesson gives you three real extracts — one from each stage — so you can hear the change, not just read about it.

The Baroque orchestra: strings, continuo and terraced dynamics

A Baroque orchestra (about 1650–1750) was built around a string section and the continuo. Grander pieces added oboes, and sometimes trumpets and timpani for ceremonial occasions, but the core sound was strings and keyboard. Because a harpsichord cannot get gradually louder — you either press a key or you do not — Baroque music often used terraced dynamics: a loud block, then a soft block, with no gradual join between them.

Strings, unlike a harpsichord, can swell in volume, and composers used that to build ceremonial grandeur. Handel’s coronation anthem Zadok the Priest opens with strings alone, playing very quietly, in a homophonic texture — rippling arpeggiated string figuration over sustained harmonies, with no independent melodic lines. Over the opening the strings build a long, gradual crescendo, getting steadily louder until the choir crashes in with a loud homophonic block of its own.

The Classical orchestra: new instruments, clearer texture

By the Classical era (about 1750–1820) the harpsichord continuo had disappeared and the orchestra had grown. Woodwind now played in pairs — flutes, oboes, bassoons, and clarinets from the 1780s — and horns were a standard section, not an occasional addition. The dense, independent lines of Baroque counterpoint gave way to clear homophonic writing: one clear melody over a simple accompaniment, built from balanced phrases of four or eight bars.

Key Fact

Classical texture is not the same as Baroque homophony. Baroque homophonic passages, like Handel’s, are blocks of chords moving together. Classical homophony is melody-and-accompaniment: one voice carries the tune while the rest support it.

Haydn’s Symphony No. 94, the ‘Surprise’ symphony, shows Classical restraint and Classical wit in the same movement. The second movement opens with the strings alone, playing a simple binary theme very quietly — two eight-bar sections, each repeated — and at the very end of the first section’s repeat, with no warning, the full orchestra crashes in on a single fortissimo chord.

That shock chord is not terraced dynamics in the Baroque sense — it is not a keyboard limitation, it is a joke. Haydn had a full dynamic range available and chose to spring it on the listener. That freedom to shape dynamics for dramatic effect, rather than because an instrument could not do otherwise, is where the Romantic era begins.

The hinge into Romanticism: Beethoven

Beethoven’s Symphony No. 1 (1800) still uses a Classical-sized orchestra, but it pushes at the edges of Classical convention. The symphony is in C major, yet its very first chord is a dominant seventh belonging to F major — the wrong key, harmonically speaking. For a few bars the listener does not know where the music actually stands. That kind of harmonic unease, used on purpose, is a taste of Romantic drama to come.

When the fast Allegro arrives, at about 1:50, the mood changes completely. The first subject is built from short, repeated motifs, pushed forward with sforzando accents and a rapid crescendo, all in a driving 2/2 alla breve.

Nothing here sounds shocking to modern ears, but in 1800 it was daring. Later Romantic composers took this same instinct — sudden accents, restless harmony, dynamics used for drama rather than decoration — and combined it with a much bigger orchestra: extra horns, valved brass, tuba, harp and a larger string section, capable of a dynamic range from a whisper to a wall of sound.

Valved brass instruments, invented in the 1810s–30s, let horns and trumpets play a full scale instead of only the notes of a bugle call. The tuba appeared in the 1830s, giving the brass section a true bass. Percussion sections grew beyond timpani to include cymbals, bass drum and more. By the later Romantic period a symphony could need over a hundred players, all available to a composer chasing an extreme of loud or soft.

Naming what you hear

In the exam you will not be told which piece is playing. You have to build the description yourself from what you hear. Start with the forces: is it strings alone, full orchestra, or something in between? Then the texture: is it contrapuntal, homophonic chords, or melody with accompaniment? Then the dynamics: is the volume shifting in sudden blocks, building gradually, or jumping with a shock accent? Naming all three, with the correct term, is worth more than saying the piece “sounds grand” or “sounds exciting”.

unit_name: Area of Study 1: Western Classical Tradition 1650–1910
lesson_title: Structures You Must Recognise: Binary, Ternary, Rondo, Variations and Sonata Form
content_html:
You already know that pieces from the classical and romantic periods are built from small musical ideas, repeated and rearranged. Composers writing between 1650 and 1910 relied on a handful of standard structures to organise a whole movement. Learn to recognise five of them — binary, ternary, rondo, theme and variations, and sonata form — and you can label the structure of almost any extract in the listening exam, even one you have never heard before.

Binary form

Binary form has two sections, usually called A and B. Both are heard once, then normally repeated immediately, so the pattern you actually hear is AABB. Section A often ends in a different key from the one it started in, and section B leads the music back home. Listen for a firm cadence — a clear stopping point — marking the end of each section, and for the same music returning almost exactly when a repeat happens.

Ternary form

Ternary form is ABA: an opening idea, a contrasting middle section, then a return of the opening. The middle section usually changes key, tempo, mood or texture, so it stands apart clearly. The giveaway is the return — when the opening tune comes back largely unchanged after the contrast, you are hearing ternary form, not just a repeat.

Rondo form

Rondo form is built from a main theme, called the refrain, that keeps coming back between contrasting sections called episodes. The pattern is often ABACA or ABACABA — the letters after A are new episodes, and each return of A is the same tune you heard first, sometimes lightly varied. The signpost is repetition: if a specific tune keeps interrupting new material, you are listening to a rondo.

Theme and variations

Theme and variations form states a theme in full, then repeats it several times with changes. Composers vary the ornamentation, the dynamics, the instrumentation, the harmony or the rhythm, while keeping the theme’s phrase structure recognisable underneath. Listen for the same underlying shape returning each time, dressed differently — a melody moved from strings to woodwind, or a plain tune gaining decoration on its repeat.

Sonata form

Sonata form is the most demanding structure in the specification. It has three main stages: exposition, development and recapitulation. The exposition presents the musical material, the development reshapes and unsettles it, and the recapitulation brings it home again — think of it as introduce, explore, resolve.

In the exposition, the first subject is stated in the home key, called the tonic. A transition passage then modulates before the second subject arrives in a contrasting key, usually the dominant if the movement is in a major key. The two subjects often contrast in character: the first energetic, the second more lyrical.

Key Fact

In a major-key sonata-form movement, the second subject arrives in the dominant key during the exposition — but returns in the tonic key in the recapitulation. That shift back to the home key is one of the clearest signposts you can listen for.

The development takes fragments of the exposition’s themes and works them through unstable, quickly-changing keys. Textures can thin out or thicken, short motifs get passed between instruments, and the harmony feels unsettled — this is the most unpredictable part of the movement.

The recapitulation restates the first and second subjects in order, but now both stay in the tonic key, resolving the tension the development created. Some movements add a short coda afterwards to round things off.

Binary: AABB — a repeat with a firm cadence at the end of each section. Ternary: ABA — a changed middle section, then an almost exact return. Rondo: a specific tune keeps coming back between new episodes. Theme and variations: the same underlying shape returns each time, dressed differently. Sonata form: two contrasting subjects that separate in key, then reunite in the tonic at the end.

In the exam, do not just name the structure — say what you heard that proves it: a returning theme, a change of key, a repeated section. That evidence is what earns the marks.

unit_name: Area of Study 1: Western Classical Tradition 1650–1910
lesson_title: Study Piece: Beethoven Symphony No. 1, Movement 1
content_html:
A symphony that starts in the wrong key

Beethoven's Symphony No. 1 in C major is the compulsory set study piece for this course. It was completed and first performed in 1800, and its opening bars already show a composer who respects the rules of the Classical symphony while quietly breaking them.

The Adagio molto opening

The movement begins with a slow Adagio molto introduction, bars 1 to 12. The very first chord is a dominant seventh chord — but it belongs in F major, not in the symphony's home key of C major. For a symphony written in 1800, opening on a chord that points away from the home key was a striking choice.

Key Fact

The Adagio molto introduction touches several harmonic areas without settling. Beethoven delays confirming C major as the tonic, so that when it finally arrives at the Allegro con brio, it lands with far more force.

Arriving in C major

This was an unusual way to begin a symphony. Most Classical symphonies before 1800 open with a clear statement of the home key, giving the listener firm ground straight away. Beethoven instead makes the listener wait for that certainty, turning the arrival of C major into an event in itself rather than a starting assumption.

Sonata form across the Allegro con brio

The main body of the movement is in sonata form. The exposition presents two contrasting ideas: a first subject in the home key, C major, followed by a second subject in a related key.

After the exposition comes the development, where Beethoven takes fragments of the exposition's themes through new keys and combinations. The recapitulation then returns to the opening themes, now settled in C major, and a coda rounds the movement off.

Exposition First subject, then second subject — then the whole exposition repeats
Development Themes fragmented and pushed through new keys
Recapitulation The themes return, now in the home key
Coda A final closing passage

Drive and energy

The Allegro con brio is in alla breve, written as 2/2. With only two strong beats per bar instead of four, the music drives forward with real momentum once it gets going.

Everything about this first subject is built for energy. Short repeated motifs give the theme its drive, sudden sforzando accents jolt the texture, and a rapid crescendo pushes the music forward. After the uncertainty of the introduction, the effect is of tension finally being released.

Orchestration: Beethoven and the wind

The symphony uses a standard late-Classical orchestra: pairs of flutes, oboes, clarinets and bassoons, pairs of horns and trumpets, timpani, and strings. Clarinets were still a relatively new addition to the symphony orchestra in 1800, and Beethoven treats the whole wind section as more than accompaniment.

Rather than simply doubling the string parts, Beethoven gives the wind instruments their own melodic material and uses them to add weight and colour at key structural moments, such as the arrival of C major at the start of the Allegro. This treatment of the wind section points forward to the far more independent orchestration of his later symphonies.

1800: inheriting Haydn and Mozart, testing the edges

Beethoven wrote his First Symphony as a former pupil of Haydn and an admirer of Mozart, and the piece uses the four-movement symphonic form, standard orchestra and sonata-form structure they had established. When it was first performed in 1800, this was still recognisably a Classical symphony.

At the same time, the harmonically unsettled opening, the sudden dynamic contrasts, and the sheer drive of the Allegro con brio show Beethoven testing what a symphony's opening could do. This is why the piece is often described as standing on the boundary between the Classical era and the Romantic era that Beethoven himself would help to create.

Writing about the set study piece

Section B marks come from three things: naming the musical element, giving its correct technical term, and saying where in the music it happens. A general impression of the music, however accurate it feels, earns little on its own.

Weak: “The music sounds exciting and grand, which shows Beethoven was a great composer.” This says nothing about the music itself — no element, no term, no location.

Strong: “The first subject, from around 1:50, creates energy through short repeated motifs and sudden sforzando accents, before a rapid crescendo drives the music forward out of the ambiguous Adagio molto introduction.” This names the passage, uses correct terms, and locates it precisely — the kind of sentence that scores full marks.

lesson_title: Rock and Pop: The Features That Give the Style Away
content_html:
In Section A of the listening exam, you may hear a short unfamiliar extract and have only seconds to work out its style. Rock and pop share a recognisable set of fingerprints: a familiar band line-up, a clear verse-chorus structure, catchy riffs and hooks, a strong backbeat, a particular rhythmic feel, and — increasingly — a production sound built in the studio rather than performed live in one take. Learn to spot each of these on its own, and you can identify the style with confidence even from a few seconds of unfamiliar audio.

The standard line-up

Most rock and pop songs are built around a core band: lead vocals carry the melody and the lyrics, electric guitar plays riffs, chords and solos, bass guitar locks in with the kick drum to drive the harmony and the groove together, and a drum kit keeps time while marking out the backbeat. Many tracks add keyboards or a synthesiser on top of this core group, filling out chords, playing countermelodies, or adding an electronic texture that a guitar and drums cannot produce alone. Hearing this combination in an unfamiliar extract — even before you can name a single instrument precisely — is one of the fastest ways to know you are listening to rock or pop rather than, say, a solo piano piece or an orchestral set work.

Verse-chorus structure

Most rock and pop songs use verse-chorus form. An intro sets the mood before the first verse arrives, verses carry the storyline and change their lyrics each time they appear, and the chorus repeats the same words and the same melody as the emotional high point of the song. Many songs also add a bridge, and a middle eight, a contrasting passage placed after the second chorus that takes the listener somewhere new — a different chord pattern, a key change, or a drop in texture — before the final chorus returns. Spotting this overall shape in an unfamiliar extract is a strong clue that you are dealing with rock or pop rather than a through-composed classical piece.

Riffs and hooks

A riff is a short repeated musical pattern, usually played by guitar or bass, that a whole song — or at least a whole section of it — is built around. A hook is whatever catches your ear and refuses to let go; it might be the riff itself, a vocal melody, or a short lyrical phrase. Riffs have driven rock since its earliest guitarists picked up distortion, and hooks remain the reason a pop chorus gets stuck in your head after a single play. In the exam, naming a riff or a hook, describing which instrument plays it, and saying roughly where it falls in the structure is worth real marks — impressions on their own are not.

The backbeat

Rock and pop rhythm sections almost always play a backbeat: an accent on beats 2 and 4 of the bar, usually struck on the snare drum, against a kick drum that typically marks beats 1 and 3. This is different from styles that place the strongest emphasis on beat 1 of the bar. Once you can hear and count the backbeat, you have one of the clearest rhythmic markers of the style available to you — it sits under almost every rock or pop track, whatever else changes around it.

Swung/shuffle vs straight feel

On top of the backbeat sits the feel — how each beat is subdivided. A straight feel splits every beat into two even parts, giving a level, marching quality. A shuffle, or swung feel, splits each beat unevenly, long-short, giving the rhythm a rolling, bouncing quality instead. The same riff or the same backbeat pattern can sound completely different depending on which feel it is played with, so training your ear to tell straight from swung subdivisions is a skill worth practising in its own right, separate from spotting the backbeat itself.

Key Fact

Always name two things when you describe rock or pop rhythm: the backbeat (beats 2 and 4) and the feel (straight or swung). Naming only one loses marks.

Production in modern pop

Much of what defines modern pop happens after the performance, in the studio. Producers build tracks from loops — short recorded or programmed sections repeated to form a beat, a bassline or a texture — and use layering to stack drums, bass, synth chords and vocal harmonies on top of each other, building the sound gradually across a track. Many pop productions use synthesised or electronic sounds instead of, or alongside, acoustic instruments, replacing a guitar riff with a synth hook or a live drum kit with a programmed beat. A steady four-on-the-floor beat, with the kick drum landing on every beat of the bar, is especially common in dance-influenced pop, because it drives a physical, danceable sense of pulse that a swung rock groove does not.

Do not expect every extract to fit neatly into one box. A track can use a live rock band line-up alongside heavily produced electronic sounds, or a pop chorus can sit over a shuffled, swung groove borrowed from rock. Listen for the individual features one at a time — line-up, structure, riff, backbeat, feel, production — and describe exactly what you hear, even when it mixes elements of both styles together.

lesson_title: Music for Stage, Screen and Games
content_html:
Music does more than decorate a story. In a musical, a film or a video game, music tells you who a character is, what they want, and how you are meant to feel about what is happening on stage or on screen. Each medium solves this problem differently, because each one places a different demand on its music: a stage musical has a fixed running order, a film has a fixed running time, and a game has neither — a player can wander, replay a level, or take three times as long as expected. Learn the vocabulary each medium uses to solve its own problem, and you can describe an unfamiliar extract from any of the three with real technical precision.

Musical theatre: songs that carry the plot

A number in a musical is rarely there just to sound nice. Early in a show, the main character often sings an “I want” song, stating their goal directly to the audience and setting the whole plot in motion — Ariel telling the audience she longs to leave the sea in “Part of Your World” is a well-known example of the type. Comic relief often arrives as a patter song, packing in as many words as the rhythm can carry for laughs rather than emotion — Gilbert and Sullivan built a whole career on them. Later, a reprise brings back an earlier melody with new lyrics, proving to the audience how far a character has travelled since we first heard that tune.

The ballad is the moment a character stops moving the plot forward and turns inward instead. It is usually slow, usually sung by a solo voice, and it exists to let the audience hear exactly what a character is feeling, unfiltered by other characters or by the action around them. Because a ballad strips almost everything else away, the voice carrying it becomes the whole performance.

Key Fact

Naming a song type is not enough on its own. Say what job it does: an “I want” song states a goal, a ballad reveals feeling, a patter song gets a laugh, a reprise shows change. The job the song does is what earns the mark.

Film score technique: leitmotif, underscore and mickey-mousing

A leitmotif is a short musical idea tied to one character, place or idea. Every time that motif returns, the composer is telling you something is present before you see it — John Williams gives Darth Vader his own leitmotif in Star Wars, and gives the shark in Jaws another, so the music alone can announce a threat the camera has not shown yet.

Most of a film score is underscore: music sitting under dialogue and action, shaping the mood of a scene without asking to be noticed. Occasionally a composer wants the opposite, and uses mickey-mousing — matching the music so precisely to an action that a rising scale tracks a character climbing, or a falling slide tracks a comic pratfall.

Tension in a score is often built with an ostinato: a short pattern repeated over and over while the composer adds instrument after instrument on top of it. Nothing about the pattern itself has to change — the tension comes from the accumulation, from the texture growing thicker and louder the longer the pattern repeats.

Diegetic and non-diegetic sound

Film sound splits into two categories. Diegetic sound exists inside the world of the story — a radio playing in the room, a band performing on screen, a character singing that other characters can hear. Non-diegetic sound exists only for the audience — the score swelling under a chase, a narrator’s voice-over — and no character in the story is aware it is playing. A film can move between the two deliberately: a song starting on a car radio, diegetic, before it swells into the full orchestral score, non-diegetic, is a common way to smooth that transition.

Game music: the loop and the layer

A film has a fixed running time and a musical has a fixed running order, so a composer always knows exactly how long a cue needs to last. A game has neither. A player might stand still for thirty seconds or three minutes, might wander back into the same room twice, might die and restart the same fight five times in a row. Game music has to loop indefinitely without becoming irritating, and it has to react to whatever the player is doing right now, not to a script that was fixed months before release.

Composers solve this by writing music in layers rather than as one fixed recording. A base loop plays constantly, and extra layers — a drum part, a countermelody, an added instrument — are switched in or out depending on what is happening in the game: exploring calmly, spotting an enemy, entering combat. This is called vertical layering, and it lets the same underlying loop feel completely different from one moment to the next without the music ever needing to stop and restart.

Section A can play you a few unfamiliar seconds from any of these three worlds. Do not try to guess the show, the film or the game — you are never marked on that. Identify the technique instead: is this a solo voice carrying a ballad, a leitmotif returning, an ostinato building under added layers, or a loop with a layer switched in? Name the technique, say exactly what you heard it do, and you have answered the question the exam is actually asking.

lesson_title: Study Piece: Queen — Bohemian Rhapsody, Seven Seas of Rhye, Love of My Life
content_html:
Queen: three set tracks, equal weight

Your study pieces are three Queen tracks: Bohemian Rhapsody, Seven Seas of Rhye and Love of My Life. Questions can ask about any of them, so know all three equally. The band: Freddie Mercury (lead vocals, piano), Brian May (electric guitar, vocals), John Deacon (bass guitar) and Roger Taylor (drum kit, vocals).

The set recordings

Key Fact — The Set Recordings

Bohemian Rhapsody and Love of My Life come from A Night at the Opera (1975). Seven Seas of Rhye comes from Queen II (1974). The set versions are the 2011 remastered recordings.

Bohemian Rhapsody: six sections, no chorus

There is no repeating chorus at all — the song is through-composed, which was very unusual for a 1970s rock single. There are four contrasting sections plus a coda. It opens a cappella, in homorhythmic block chords. A piano ballad follows, with arpeggiated accompaniment.

Then come a virtuosic guitar solo, an opera section, a hard rock section, and a quiet, reflective outro.

Bohemian Rhapsody: keys and metre

The a cappella opening and the ballad are both in B flat major — the very first chord is B flat 6, an unusual added-sixth chord. The rock section that follows the opera is in E flat major. The opera section jumps to A major, an unrelated key — that jump is a modulation. The song then ends on an F major chord. That is the dominant of the opening key of B flat major, which is why the ending feels unfinished.

The hard rock section shifts into 12/8, a compound time signature. The rest is almost all 4/4 — except single bars of 5/4 and 9/8 in the introduction.

Bohemian Rhapsody: the voices

Mercury had a four-octave range and uses all of it: soaring falsetto in some places, belted chest voice in others. The word-setting is almost entirely syllabic. Listen for portamento slides on words like ‘reality’, a Scotch snap on ‘sympathy’, and word painting as the melody rises at the line about looking up.

In the opera section the ‘Galileo’ motif uses repeated notes and a rising semitone. ‘Bismillah!’ works as question and answer: the refusal line lands in octaves, and the group replies in homophonic chords.

Bohemian Rhapsody: built in the studio

Key Fact — The Recording

Bohemian Rhapsody was built in the studio. It uses roughly 180 vocal overdubs, bounced across tape generations. The song could not be performed live as recorded.

Brian May’s guitar solo at the end of the ballad is virtuosic, with fast scalic passages, slides, bends, vibrato and distortion. In the opera section the drums play the same rhythms as the voices rather than a steady beat, and the staccato crotchet opening imitates the comic characters of real opera.

Bohemian Rhapsody: the studio sound

Production is part of the analysis. There is heavy electric guitar overdubbing. The vocals are panned across the stereo field, most clearly in the opera section. Dynamics swing from alternating quiet and loud phrases to fortissimo interjections, before the final fall away to piano.

Seven Seas of Rhye: the first hit

A hard rock song in D major. Released in February 1974, it was the single that made Queen’s name. It opens with a ten-bar piano introduction: an arpeggiated riff in octaves, in semiquavers. The verse hits with power chords underneath.

After the bridge and a guitar solo, the song dissolves into a music-hall singalong — ‘I Do Like to Be Beside the Seaside’ — played on a stylophone, a completely different style to end on. There is no chorus anywhere: instead a vocal hook closes each verse.

Seven Seas of Rhye: sounds to name

The guitar solo moves to B flat major before returning to D, and the second bridge modulates to G major. Three more details to name: power chords in the introduction; blues notes colouring the vocal line; palm-muting in the first bridge; and a delay effect at the end of the guitar solo.

The bridge is the contrast section. The mode shifts, a new melody breaks the verse pattern, and it ends with a long held vocal cry that launches the guitar solo.

Love of My Life: the ballad

The ballad of the three. Home is F major, but the harmony travels constantly — naming where it goes is where the marks are. The short introduction implies F major, then slips to B flat major in its second phrase.

The two verses start in C major and modulate to F major. An instrumental bridge in B flat major then echoes that second phrase of the introduction.

Love of My Life: the journey home

The harp is played by Brian May, who taught himself the instrument for this song — an orchestral harp is not a normal rock-band sound. An interlude turns to D minor — the relative minor — passing through G minor on the way.

The guitar solo begins in F major, moves to C major, then B flat major. The coda starts in D minor and finishes in F major: the song only settles at home in its last bars.

Love of My Life: sonority and texture

Sonority is the topic to reach for here. Mercury sings in his tenor range, with moments of falsetto. Around him sit layered backing vocals, harp and arpeggiated piano.

If a question asks about texture or timbre, this is the track to choose.

Three structures, one exam topic

The spread is deliberate. One multi-sectional epic that breaks the rules of song form. One compact hard rock single. One ballad.

Comparisons almost write themselves: no chorus in two of the three; piano-led against guitar-led; studio construction against near-live simplicity. Revise them side by side, not one at a time.

Writing about the tracks

Marks come from three things: name the element, give its exact technical term, and say where in the track it happens. ‘The harmony is interesting’ earns nothing.

‘The opera section shifts abruptly to A major, an unrelated key’ earns — element, term, location.

lesson_title: Placing a Track in Time: Rock, Pop, Broadway and Screen by Era
content_html:
Why the date matters

Section A plays you music you have never heard. The question is not only “what can you hear?” but “where does this belong?” Your exam covers four areas of popular music, and each is tied to a period: Broadway from the 1950s to the 1990s, rock of the 1960s and 1970s, film and computer gaming music from the 1990s onwards, and pop from the 1990s onwards.

You are not asked to guess the year. You are asked to hear the features that belong to a period and name them. This lesson gives you those features.

Rock of the 1960s and 1970s

The clearest clue is that the band sounds like people playing together in a room, because that is usually how it was recorded. The tempo breathes slightly instead of staying machine-exact. Drums are acoustic and you can hear the room around them.

Listen for electric guitar with overdrive or fuzz, the Hammond organ or electric piano, and a bass guitar playing a real line rather than a synthesised one. Vocals are often double-tracked, but never pitch-corrected.

Structures are verse and chorus with room for an instrumental solo. Later in the 1970s some rock grows more ambitious: longer forms, changes of metre and whole album sides given to one piece.

Key Fact — The Timing Test

Ask yourself whether the drums are perfectly even. Human drumming pushes and pulls very slightly. A grid-exact beat almost always means programming, which points to the 1990s or later.

Pop from the 1990s to now

Modern pop is built rather than performed. Drums are programmed or sampled and quantised, so the beat does not drift. Underneath sit synthesiser pads and bass, and often a loop that runs through the whole track.

Vocals are the giveaway. They are layered, close-recorded and heavily treated, and from the late 1990s onwards you may hear pitch correction. Everything is compressed so the whole track sits loud and level.

Structure is tighter than in older rock: a short introduction, verse, a pre-chorus, then the chorus, often with a stripped-back middle section before the last one.

Broadway from the 1950s to the 1990s

Broadway spans fifty years, so listen for where in that span an extract sits. The 1950s bring a large pit orchestra with lush strings and a singing style closer to the classical tradition. Songs carry the plot: an opening number that sets the scene, and a song where the main character states what they want.

From the 1960s and 1970s, rock and pop instruments arrive in the pit — drum kit, electric guitar, electric bass. By the 1980s and 1990s you meet the big sung-through musical: little or no spoken dialogue, amplified voices, synthesisers alongside the orchestra, and themes that return across the whole show.

Film and gaming music from the 1990s

Orchestral scoring never went away, and a full orchestra with leitmotifs remains common. What marks out the modern period is the blend: orchestra layered with synthesisers, electronic percussion and sound design, and driving ostinato patterns under action scenes.

Game music has one feature film music does not need. It cannot know how long a scene will last, so it is written to loop seamlessly, and it often changes in layers — instruments are added or removed as the action intensifies rather than the music simply stopping and starting.

Putting it together in the exam

Name the feature, then let it place the extract. “The drums are programmed and exactly on the grid, and the vocal is layered and pitch-corrected, so this is pop from the 1990s or later” earns marks twice over: it describes the music and it supplies the context.

lesson_title: Traditional Music: The Four Styles You Must Recognise
content_html:
What “Traditional Music” Means in This Exam

Traditional music covers two things on this specification. The first is music that takes its influences from traditional sources — folk music, for example — and reworks them in a modern style. The second is traditional music from its own culture, performed as it was meant to be performed. Both count, and both turn up in the listening paper.

You will meet four styles, and you are expected to recognise each one from a short extract you have never heard before: blues from 1920 to 1950, fusion music drawing on African and/or Caribbean music, contemporary Latin music, and contemporary folk music of the British Isles.

Reading about these styles is not enough. Each section below gives you the features examiners look for, and then an extract so you can hear the feature straight away. Play every extract. The point is to attach a word to a sound, so that when the sound turns up in the exam the word comes back to you.

Blues, 1920–1950

Blues is built on repetition. Most blues songs follow the twelve-bar blues — a twelve-bar chord pattern using chords I, IV and V that repeats for the whole song. Once you hear the pattern come round again, you have found it.

Three other features give blues away. The rhythm is usually swung, so the beat divides unevenly into a long-short lilt rather than straight halves. The singer is answered by an instrument in call and response. And the melody bends certain notes flat — the blue notes — which is where the style gets its characteristic sound.

Key Fact

If you can hear a chord pattern returning to the start every twelve bars, and the beat has an uneven long-short swing, you are almost certainly listening to blues.

Fusion with African and Caribbean Music

Fusion means two traditions meeting. In this strand, African or Caribbean musical thinking meets a contemporary style, and the result usually shows it in the rhythm section rather than the tune.

Listen for guitars playing short repeated patterns that lock together rather than strumming as one, and for percussion layered so that different parts pull against each other. That pull is cross-rhythm, and it is the single most reliable sign of this strand. In Caribbean styles you will often hear the chords land on the offbeat, which is what gives reggae and ska their lift.

Contemporary Latin Music

Latin music is percussion-led. Congas, bongos and timbales layer up under a piano riff called the montuno, and brass adds short punched chords on top. Underneath it all sits the clave, a five-note rhythmic pattern that the whole band organises itself around.

Latin songs also have a distinctive structure. A lead singer improvises a line and the group answers with a fixed repeated phrase — the coro. It is call and response again, but arranged differently from blues: the group answer stays the same while the lead line changes.

Contemporary Folk of the British Isles

British and Irish folk melodies often sit in a mode rather than a straightforward major or minor key, which is why they can sound neither happy nor sad but somewhere else entirely. Underneath the tune you will often hear a drone, a held note that never moves.

The other giveaway is decoration. A folk player rarely repeats a tune identically. On the repeat they add ornamentation — quick grace notes and rolls threaded through the melody. Dance tunes such as jigs also move in compound time, with the beat dividing into three rather than two, which produces their characteristic bounce.

Writing About What You Hear

Recognising a style earns you nothing unless you can say why. Examiners want the technical word, not an impression. “It sounds happy and bouncy” scores nothing; “the melody is decorated with grace notes over a drone, in compound time” scores.

Use this three-step habit for any listening answer. Name the element the question asks about. Give the technical term for what that element is doing. Say where in the extract you heard it. For example: “The texture is call and response — the guitar answers each sung phrase throughout the extract.”

Twelve-bar blues, swung rhythm, blue note, call and response, cross-rhythm, offbeat chords, clave, montuno, coro, drone, modal melody, ornamentation, compound time. Each of these names something you can point to in a recording — which is exactly what an examiner is asking you to do.

lesson_title: Study Piece: Esperanza Spalding — I Know You Know, Little Fly, I Adore You
content_html:
Your Section B choice

Your second set of study pieces is three tracks by Esperanza Spalding, an American jazz bassist, singer and composer. Two come from her album Esperanza (2008): I Know You Know and I Adore You. The third, Little Fly, comes from Chamber Music Society (2010).

The set recordings

Key Fact — The Set Recordings

I Know You Know and I Adore You (Esperanza, 2008) fuse jazz with samba. Little Fly (Chamber Music Society, 2010) sets a William Blake poem for voice, double bass and string trio.

All three tracks are fusions. They mix jazz harmony and improvisation, Brazilian samba rhythm and — in Little Fly — chamber-music strings. In 2011 Spalding became the first jazz artist to win the Grammy for Best New Artist.

Little Fly: a poem set for strings

The words are William Blake’s poem ‘The Fly’. The scoring is chamber music: voice, pizzicato double bass, and a string trio of violin, viola and cello. That makes four string instruments — but it is not a string quartet, and naming that difference exactly earns marks.

The structure follows Blake’s poem and is strophic: an introduction, then two verses, then a coda. Verses one and two of the poem make the song’s first verse, verses three and four make the second, and the poem’s last verse becomes the coda.

Little Fly: the riff and the voice

Everything grows from the bass riff in the introduction: a chromatically descending line played pizzicato, using double stopping. In verse one the riff carries on without the double stopping, then stops altogether. The riff returns about twenty times — forty of the piece’s sixty-three bars.

The voice moves mostly by step and sets the words syllabically. Each verse opens with a descending three-note pattern in E major, repeated. At each verse-end the word ‘oh’ falls in three chromatic steps.

Little Fly: verse two and the coda

Verse two adds a violin countermelody and interjections from the ensemble, and the viola recalls its own melody from the introduction. The trio normally plays arco, but in the coda all three play pizzicato. A bass improvisation follows, then the voice returns scatting in dialogue with it, over a sustained string chord. Spalding sings in the alto range, moving into head voice with vibrato in the second half of each verse, and the strings use trills to suggest the fly.

I Know You Know: samba-jazz with a secret

A samba-jazz song in verse-chorus form, with improvisation sections built in. Its harmonic trick is simple to say in an exam: the home key of F major is hidden until the chorus.

The track opens with a monophonic texture — a solo fretless bass riff. The riff avoids the first beat of every one of its seventeen bars. The chords that join it dodge the chord of F, and the first sung note is G — the supertonic.

I Know You Know: the chorus and the rhythm

The chorus finally lands on F major through the jazz progression ii–V–I — G minor 7, C7, F — with every chord carrying a seventh. The chorus melody adds blue notes, especially A flat and D flat.

The samba lives in the rhythm section: ganza (a shaker), caixa (a Brazilian snare drum) and a triangle. Off-beat piano chords in the chorus create a double-time samba feel. Syncopations layer into polyrhythm.

I Know You Know: the interlude

The interlude modulates to the distant key of B major, with a vamp for piano and bass solos. Then it snaps back to F for a double chorus. Production is light but nameable: some reverb, panning and EQ.

I Know You Know: the hidden tonic

Key Fact — The Hidden Tonic

The bass riff opens on dominant Cs, the chords avoid F, and the voice enters on G. F major is only confirmed by the first chord of the chorus — naming that moment is a ready-made exam answer.

I Adore You: scat, samba and a mode

This track has almost no conventional lyrics. The voice works in scat and vocalise throughout. The spoken rhythm of the title phrase forms the main melodic hook.

It opens and closes with unpitched samba percussion — surdo and ocean drum among them. The piece literally begins and ends in no key at all. Even when pitch arrives, the tonality stays ambiguous, with dissonant piano interjections against the voice.

I Adore You: structure and mode

The main groove settles into G mixolydian. The track fades out on percussion alone, so no final chord ever confirms a key — a strong exam sentence.

Structure is sectional: a main groove, verses and a bridge that repeat and develop. The solo section is long: the piano improvises first over drums and bass, then the voice and double bass take over together. These improvisations are far more extensive than in the other two tracks.

I Adore You: metre and bass

The metre is the feature to name: the music alternates between 3/4 for the introductions and main groove and 2/4 for the verses and bridges, switching back and forth throughout — unusual for samba, which normally stays in 2/4 or 4/4. The low end here is double bass, where I Know You Know uses fretless bass guitar.

Why does this count as traditional music?

Area of Study 3 includes fusions that reinterpret traditional sources in a modern style. These tracks are exactly that: samba percussion from Brazil, blues-derived notes and jazz harmony from the African-American tradition, and — in Little Fly — an English poem set with chamber strings.

In Section B, frame every observation as a fusion of named traditions. That framing lifts an answer into the top band.

Writing about the tracks

Marks come from three things: name the element, give its exact term, and say where in the track it happens. ‘The music feels floaty’ earns nothing. ‘The introduction of I Know You Know withholds the tonic until the chorus’ earns everything.

Anchor each track to one signature fact: the twenty returns of Little Fly’s riff with its inverted G sharp pedal; the hidden-then-revealed F major of I Know You Know; and the mode, scat and keyless percussion frame of I Adore You.

unit_name: Area of Study 4: Western Classical Tradition since 1910
lesson_title: Twentieth-Century Colour: Orchestration, Dynamics and Space
content_html:
A New Sound World

Before 1910, most classical music built its effect from melody, harmony and rhythm, in that order. Tone colour mattered, but it served the tune underneath it. After 1910, many composers began treating timbre itself as a subject worth composing with, not just a wrapper around a melody. The choice of instrument became part of the musical idea, not an afterthought.

This shows up first in orchestration. Composers picked unusual instrument pairings, extreme registers and exposed solo colours precisely because of how they sounded, not just because of the notes they played. A phrase given to a bassoon high in its range, or to a solo flute over hushed strings, means something different from the same phrase given to a full string section — even if every pitch is identical.

Key Fact

The same melody can sound completely different depending on which instrument plays it, how loudly, and how many other parts surround it — twentieth-century composers built entire pieces around exploiting this.

Open Space versus Dense Texture

Composers also began treating texture as an expressive choice in its own right. A texture can be widely spaced and open — a single melodic line with only a few sustained notes underneath, and a wide gap between the highest and lowest parts — or dense and layered, with many independent lines crowding the same registers at once. Neither approach is better than the other; each creates a completely different sound world, and composers moved between them for contrast.

Long-Range Control of Dynamics

Twentieth-century composers also stretched dynamics to extremes, and controlled them over long spans of time rather than just from phrase to phrase. Instead of one sudden forte, a passage might begin at the edge of audibility and build, bar by bar, across several minutes, in one continuous crescendo towards a huge climax. That long-range shape is itself a structural device, not just a passing effect — it can hold an entire movement together.

Jazz and Popular Idioms Enter the Concert Hall

Jazz and blues, both new popular styles in the early twentieth century, fed directly into concert music. Composers borrowed sliding pitches, bent notes and syncopated rhythms from jazz players and wrote them straight into orchestral scores. A blue note or a smooth upward slide can bring a whole jazz atmosphere into a symphony orchestra without a single jazz musician on stage.

The Wind Band as a Serious Concert Medium

The wind band had long existed for marches and military occasions. In the twentieth century, composers began writing original concert works for it, treating it as a serious medium with its own palette of colours — bright massed brass, reedy woodwind choirs, a full percussion section — rather than as a cheaper substitute for a full orchestra.

Loosening Tonality

Traditional tonal music treats dissonance as tension that must resolve to consonance. After 1910, many composers loosened this rule. Harmony often still points to a home key, but it can be extended tonality: chords built from added and stacked notes, not just plain triads. Others turned to modal scales borrowed from folk music or earlier eras for a different flavour entirely. Crucially, dissonance itself became a colour to enjoy, not a problem that always needed fixing.

Not quite. Fully atonal music, including twelve-note serialism, abandons a home key altogether. Extended tonality and modality are gentler: the music still points towards a tonal centre, but reaches it by a wider, more colourful route than strict major-minor harmony allows.

Putting the Picture Together

When an unfamiliar extract from this period comes up in the exam, run through these five clues. Is timbre doing more than decorating a tune? Is the texture wide open or densely packed? Are the dynamics building over a long span rather than jumping suddenly? Is there any trace of jazz or blues? Could the forces be a wind band rather than a full orchestra? And does the harmony still feel tonal, even though it does not behave like a textbook major or minor key? Naming two or three of these, with the correct technical term, is worth more marks than a general impression.

unit_name: Area of Study 4: Western Classical Tradition since 1910
content_html:
Bartók, the folk-song collector

Béla Bartók did not just compose from imagination. From 1906 he travelled through remote villages in Hungary and Romania, and later further afield, with a phonograph, recording peasants singing their oldest songs. He and his friend Zoltán Kodály wrote thousands of these melodies down by hand, comparing versions and sorting them by type.

How fieldwork changed his music

That fieldwork changed his own composing. Village singers rarely used the plain major or minor scales of a piano lesson. Bartók heard old modal scales, short phrases repeated and varied rather than developed at length, and rhythms locked to the steps of a dance. All three habits carried straight into his own concert music, including Hungarian Sketches.

Bartók grouped the tunes he collected into an “old style” — pentatonic, freely sung, without regular bar lines — and a “new style” shaped by newer dance forms with a steadier beat. Hungarian Sketches draws on both: slow, speech-like rubato melody in one movement, driving dance rhythm in the next.

Hungarian Sketches: five pictures, four for your exam

Hungarian Sketches, Magyar Képek, or “Hungarian Pictures”, is an orchestral suite Bartók put together in 1931 from five short piano pieces he had written roughly twenty years earlier. Each movement is a small “picture” of Hungarian rural life — a village at dusk, a dance, a drunk stumbling home.

The four movements you need

Key Fact

Your exam asks for four of the five movements: 1 Evening in the Village, 2 Bear Dance, 4 Slightly Tipsy, and 5 Swineherd’s Dance. Movement 3, Melody, is not on the specification — do not spend revision time on it.

Orchestration with a light touch

Hungarian Sketches is written for orchestra — woodwind including piccolo, bass clarinet and contrabassoon, horns, trumpets, trombones and tuba, timpani, percussion including side drums, triangle, cymbals and bass drum, and strings — but used with a light touch.

Evening in the Village uses only woodwind, two horns and strings. Bartók keeps much of the texture thin, often just a solo woodwind line over a handful of accompanying instruments, so each “picture” keeps the intimate feel of a folk tune rather than a big symphonic statement.

Precision about sonority

What examiners reward here is Bartók’s precision about sonority. The strings switch constantly between bowed playing and pizzicato, add fast tremolo for shimmer, play muted (con sordino) and are even asked to play ruvido — coarsely.

The brass mute and unmute; the triangle player is told to use a metal beater. Almost every note of the woodwind melodies carries an articulation instruction. That level of detailed instruction about instrumental colour and dynamics is a signature of the piece — and a ready-made Section B answer.

Snap rhythms and folk-dance patterns

A snap rhythm is a very short, accented note followed by a longer one. It gives a dance an off-balance, kicking feel.

It comes straight from the rhythm of spoken Hungarian and of Hungarian folk dance steps. The dance movements drive differently — on short repeated ostinato figures that keep the dance driving forward.

Evening in the Village (Movement 1)

The movement is in arch form — A, B, A1, B1, A2 — a symmetry Bartók was known for. The A sections are marked Lento rubato, slow and speech-like. The B sections are Allegretto, nearly twice the speed.

A1 brings the slow music back varied, B1 the quick music with trills added, and A2 closes the arch. It is mostly 4/4, but bars of 3/4 and 2/4 near the end unsettle the ending.

Evening in the Village: mode, melody and texture

Both melodies come from the F sharp minor pentatonic scale, and the A section uses the Aeolian mode on F sharp. Both were typical of the folk music Bartók collected.

The A melody is mainly a descending legato phrase — the musical equivalent of a sigh at the end of the day. The B melody is the opposite: staccato, conjunct quavers over short pizzicato, so not everyone’s evening is calm.

Texture is melody and accompaniment, with different woodwind taking the solo line over chordal accompaniment — either long held notes or pizzicato crotchets. Dynamics run from ppp to forte. Bartók avoids traditional cadences and uses non-functional chords, so the key stays deliberately unclear.

Bear Dance (Movement 2)

Bartók described this movement as the impression of a bear dancing to its leader’s song, growling to a drum. It is in varied strophic form, and the easiest way to hear the sections is to follow the pedal note.

A sits on a D pedal in cellos, basses, horns and tuba. B moves the pedal to A flat in the second violins — D to A flat is a tritone. Then A1, B1 and A2 complete the symmetry. The movement ends on a D major chord.

Bear Dance: mode, forces and rhythm

The melody of A is based on the Aeolian mode on D sharp; B uses the Lydian dominant scale on D. Phrases are mostly four bars long and deliberately dissonant, which is what gives the dance its excitement.

Bartók adds two trumpets, two trombones, tuba, contrabassoon, timpani and two side drums to the forces of the first movement. The side drums start without snares and switch them on for B. A triangle appears in A1, the brass sometimes play muted, and the strings both bow and pluck.

Bear Dance: texture and rhythm

Texture revolves around the pedal notes, which act as a rhythmic drone. The melody is harmonised in thirds, sixths and octaves and moves in block chords. Repeated quavers in the pedal and snare drum build the anticipation, while the melody moves mainly in crotchets — the rhythm of the Hungarian kanász folk dance. Dynamics run from piano to forte with sforzando stabs, and there is a great deal of staccato.

Slightly Tipsy (Movement 4)

True to its title, this movement portrays someone stumbling rather than walking in a straight line. It is in ternary form: an opening A section, a contrasting B section, then a return of A that is significantly developed rather than simply repeated.

Almost every note of the opening melody is decorated with acciaccaturas — the single feature that most creates the tipsy feel. The opening melody is built on the interval of a perfect fourth; the second motif descends by step.

Slightly Tipsy: sound and texture

Sonority is mostly woodwind and strings. The strings sometimes play col legno, and at the start they are muted and told to play at the tip of the bow for a thin, quiet sound.

Tonality is deliberately ambiguous. It begins major, and the B section moves to G minor, with parallel chords, chromatic harmony and dissonant added-note chords.

The marking is Allegretto rubato, so the music speeds up and slows down. It is mostly 4/4, but a few bars of 2/4 and one bar of 5/4 unsettle the phrasing. Dynamics run from pianissimo to forte with sudden changes, and slur-staccato articulation makes the music sway.

Swineherd’s Dance (Movement 5)

The suite ends with the only genuine collected folk tune in it. Bartók recorded it in Tolna County in 1907. This movement has more sections than any other here. It opens with an introduction over a drone, with fragments of the tune appearing before it properly arrives.

The first half of the folk melody enters, then the second half. Both halves come back changed: a reworked second half, a four-bar link, then the first half again. After a three-bar link the second half is fragmented and developed, with its final two bars held back — the coda is built on exactly those two bars.

Swineherd’s Dance: mode and sound

The tonal centre is A, set by the drone, and the mode is mixolydian on A. The B section shifts its drone to D before returning to A, and G sharps in its second half lean towards G major.

The melody opens with leaps of fourths and fifths, then moves by step, and sits quite high. The woodwind carry it — piccolo, flute, oboe and clarinet — over strings playing both bowed and pizzicato, muted and unmuted. At the very end two solo violins play harmonics.

Swineherd’s Dance: metre and rhythm

The metre is 2/4 throughout and the marking is Allegro molto: quick and lively, with moments of calm and changes of tempo. An ostinato rhythm — quaver, crotchet, quaver — drives many sections, and the horns and trumpets have syncopated melodies. Dynamics run from pianissimo to fortissimo with many crescendos and diminuendos.

Writing about Hungarian Sketches in Section B

Section B marks come from three things, in this order: name the musical element or technique, give the correct technical term for it, and say exactly where in the movement it happens. “Bartók uses folk music” earns nothing on its own. “Bartók builds the Allegretto dance tune of Evening in the Village on scotch-snap rhythms” earns marks, because it names the feature, uses the right term, and locates it.

Practise building answers in that order for each of the four required movements, and keep the ostinato and scotch-snap vocabulary ready — and make sure each one is attached to the right movement.

unit_name: Area of Study 4: Western Classical Tradition since 1910
content_html:
Minimalism: process instead of themes

Minimalism is one of the four listening strands in Area of Study 4. In the exam you might hear an unfamiliar extract and have to recognise it as minimalism within seconds, so you need to know what the technique actually sounds like, not just its name.

Area of Study 1 trained you to listen for themes and their development in sonata form. Minimalism works the opposite way: there is no theme to develop. A composer sets up a short musical idea and a rule for changing it, then lets that rule run. The structure you hear is the process itself, not a plot of themes coming and going.

Key Fact

Minimalism builds pieces from a steady pulse and short repeated cells, changed by a process such as addition or phasing, instead of from themes that are stated and developed.

Every minimalist extract you hear rests on two constants: a pulse that never lets up, and a cell — a short pattern repeated over and over. Everything else in this lesson is a way of changing that cell over time.

Adams, Reich and Riley are all in copyright, so the links below open official recordings on the performers’ or label’s own channels rather than audio hosted here.

The additive process — Terry Riley

In an additive process, a cell grows by one note at a time: play it, add a note, play the new version, add another note, and the pattern lengthens in front of you. Terry Riley’s In C works differently — built not on note-by-note growth but on staggered repetition. It is not one fixed melody but 53 short numbered patterns; every player in the ensemble repeats each pattern as many times as they like before moving to the next, so the players drift in and out of step with each other and no two performances ever match.

A performance of In C typically runs anywhere from forty-five to ninety minutes — far too long for a revision session. Play a few minutes instead, with the additive process in mind.

  • Terry Riley, In C (Bang on a Can All-Stars) — each player moves through the 53 numbered patterns at their own pace, so listen for the ensemble sliding in and out of alignment as a result.

Phasing and gradual change — Steve Reich

Steve Reich’s signature technique is phasing: two players start an identical pattern together, then one very gradually pulls ahead until the two lines lock into a new relationship. Reich built entire pieces from this single idea. In large ensemble works such as Music for 18 Musicians, that same instinct for extremely gradual, almost imperceptible change is stretched across a much bigger canvas: pulsing chords, tuned percussion parts that interlock note against note in a technique called hocket, and a very slow harmonic rhythm that only shifts every few minutes.

Music for 18 Musicians runs to roughly an hour, so do not attempt the whole piece. Pick any five minutes and listen for how little happens, and how gradually it happens — that slowness is the point, not a flaw.

  • Steve Reich, Music for 18 Musicians — sample any five minutes and notice how little changes, and how gradually it changes.

Layering and texture — John Adams

A minimalist texture rarely arrives all at once. Layer after layer is added on top of the pulse, thickening the sound until a listener notices the piece has quietly built from a bare few instruments into a full ensemble. This layering is easiest to hear when a piece is short enough to take in whole. John Adams’ Short Ride in a Fast Machine lasts about four minutes, which makes it the most immediately graspable of the three pieces in this lesson and a good place to start.

  • John Adams, Short Ride in a Fast Machine (Berliner Philharmoniker) — at under four minutes this is the clearest introduction to the whole technique, so start here before the longer pieces.

Sonata form states a theme, develops it through fragmentation and key change, then restates it. Minimalism states a cell, changes it through a process such as addition or phasing, and lets that process — not a return to the opening idea — carry the structure. If an extract has a clear tune that comes back transformed, think sonata form. If it has a short pattern repeating and mutating with almost no melody to speak of, think minimalism.

Why this matters in the exam

Section A of the listening exam plays short unfamiliar extracts and asks you to identify and describe what you hear. Marks come from naming the element, giving the correct technical term, and saying where in the extract it happened — not from a vague impression that the music “sounds repetitive”. Write “additive process” or “phasing”, not “it keeps going”.
